title: Al-Muzzammil, whole
hookLine: the night prayer and measured recitation (Surah 73)
tomorrow: why would anyone feed a stranger and refuse a thank-you?

cards: The hoodie pulled all the way over the head, the blanket over the face: the oldest way to tell the world, not now. There's a story with a blanket in it. A man comes home from a cave on a mountain, his heart pounding.
Sahih al-Bukhari records what he says to his wife, Khadijah: cover me, cover me. She wraps him up and stays with him until the fear leaves.
The man is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and something has just spoken to him in that cave. A surah of the Qur'an opens by calling him exactly that: the wrapped one. You'd expect the next word to be rest.

teach.b: In Pickthall's words, it opens: "O thou wrapped up in thy raiment!" And then, instead of rest: rise.

Stand in the night, all of it but a little, half, or a bit less, or a bit more, "and chant the Qur'an in measured form." The Arabic word for that is tartil: slow, even, each word given its own place. Not a cram.
Not a scroll. Then the surah gives a reason, and it's the detail to tell a friend tonight.

teach.h: THE NIGHT LEAVES A DEEPER MARK.
teach.b: It says the hours of the night leave a deeper mark, and words said then come out straighter. Anyone who has typed a message at two in the morning knows the night changes how words land.
This surah aims that weight at something worth saying. And here's the turn the story has been waiting for. The surah's last verse comes back to the night and softens it.
Your Lord knows you stand nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third. He knows some of you are sick, some traveling to earn a living, some fighting in His cause.
So recite what is easy of it. Some commentators hold that this verse came down later than the opening. Either way, the surah keeps both in one place, the call and the mercy.
The wrapped one is told to get up. Not forever, and not perfectly.
Stand, recite, slowly, as much as is easy.

how: Muslims who keep a voluntary night prayer (tahajjud or qiyam al-layl) rise after some sleep and recite slowly in it; Surah al-Muzzammil is read as one of its foundations.

o: the night sky: a surah naming the stars and moon
the wrapped one: a surah calling him to rise at night
the cloaked rider: a title for a traveling messenger

games.q: the surah, piece by piece — tap the pairs.

s: the surah commands praying the whole night, every night
it says stand the night but a little, about half, and its last verse eases it: recite what is easy.
the surah gives a reason for the night
the hours of the night leave a deeper mark, and speech is straighter then (73:6).
night recitation should go as fast as possible to cover more
the command is measured recitation, each word given its place.

games.q: your cousin starts a night-prayer habit, reads for two hours on night one, and quits by night four. you're up late too. what does al-Muzzammil suggest?
o: read even longer to make up for the nights you missed.
a little, slowly, that you can keep: what is easy.
wait until life is calm enough to do it properly.
games.why: the surah's own ending turns to mercy: God knows people are sick, traveling, working. recite what is easy of it.

practice: If you can, stand up where you are, feet steady, hands loose at your sides. Say aloud, slowly, any short line you know by heart, a verse, a surah, or simply a name of God, giving each word its own breath.
Then stay standing in the quiet for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-Muzzammil: the wrapped one. The name of Surah 73, which tells the one under the blanket to rise in the night and recite, slowly.

orig.note: Arabic: the one wrapped up; the surah's opening address and its name.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: stand, recite, only what's easy, and slowly. Al-Muzzammil, read by night.
